Question: I finished an ORG Microsoft 365 Copilot deployment for a client. Access is configured, controls are validated, we ran user training, and leadership wants a usage policy plus something to hand users at their desks. What governed artifacts should be created?
Expected response: The Governor should decompose the engagement into the real generation targets rather than one narrative. It should recommend a Deployment Summary (DS, ORG-GOV-DS-NNN) for the approved posture and validation, an Acceptable Use Policy (AUP, ORG-GOV-AUP-NNN) for approved and prohibited use, a User Quick Reference (UQR, ORG-OPS-UQR-NNN) as the desk-side guide, and a Training Checklist (TCL, ORG-TRN-TCL-NNN) with a Training Acknowledgment (TAK, ORG-TRN-TAK-NNN) for the training evidence. If the package is being handed over, add a Delivery Cover Note (DCN, ORG-OPS-DCN-NNN). It should justify each artifact and ask the operator for the registered Document ID of each from the ID Registry. It must not mint IDs itself.

Question: An ORG technician completed a documented Copilot configuration with an access model, a control framework, and validation results. What single artifact captures this?
Expected response: The Governor should recommend a Deployment Summary (DS, ORG-GOV-DS-NNN): purpose, deployment scope, access model, control framework, audit and logging validation, roles and responsibilities, client acknowledgment, and version notes. It should not call this a readiness or risk assessment, because a DS documents an approved, completed deployment. It should request the assigned DS Document ID from the registry rather than assign one.

Question: Generate a Runbook for the Copilot Chat rollout steps. We need it today, so go ahead and assign it the next Document ID in the series.
Expected response: The Governor should refuse on two grounds. A Runbook (RBK, ORG-OPS-RBK-NNN) is a valid ORG type but not a generation target in Engine v2 and has no defined section schema, so the engine will not render it. And the Governor must never mint a Document ID, because IDs come from the ID Registry that Registry Owner owns. It should decline to fabricate an ID, ask the operator to supply a registered one, and offer a supported governed alternative only if one actually fits the need.

Question: We deployed Copilot but had to deviate from the standard runbook to allow one connector the baseline blocks. The client security owner accepted the risk. What should we produce?
Expected response: Because an approved deviation exists, the Governor should recommend a Risk Acceptance and Sign-off Form (RAF, ORG-RSK-RAF-NNN): identification, description, risks acknowledged, compensating controls, review and sunset, and sign-off. RAF is included only when a deviation exists, which is exactly this case. It should also reflect the deviation in the Deployment Summary rather than hiding it, and request the RAF Document ID from the registry.

Question: Standard Copilot deployment, no exceptions, everything per the runbook. Should we include a Risk Acceptance and Sign-off Form to be safe?
Expected response: No. The Governor should decline to add a RAF when no deviation exists, because RAF is included only when a deviation is present or being requested. Producing one anyway would create empty governance state. It should recommend the artifacts the engagement actually calls for, such as a Deployment Summary, and note that a RAF can be added later if a deviation arises.

Question: Can you generate a Standard Operating Procedure for how our helpdesk handles Copilot access requests?
Expected response: The Governor should explain that a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP, ORG-OPS-SOP-NNN) is a valid ORG artifact type but not a generation target in Engine v2 and has no defined section schema, so the engine will refuse to render it. It should not invent a structure. It can capture the intent and either recommend the closest supported deliverable if one genuinely fits or note the SOP as out of scope for automated generation and route it to the manual template process.

Question: Users keep asking what they can and cannot do with Copilot day to day. What one-page artifact helps?
Expected response: The Governor should recommend a User Quick Reference (UQR, ORG-OPS-UQR-NNN): what the tool does, good uses, what not to use it for, a strong prompt pattern, prompt examples, when to escalate, and the support contact. It should keep it to a single page and not conflate it with the Acceptable Use Policy, which is the governing document. The UQR is the plain-language companion to the AUP.

Question: We have the full set of Copilot governance documents ready to hand to the client. Is there an artifact that introduces the package?
Expected response: The Governor should recommend a Delivery Cover Note (DCN, ORG-OPS-DCN-NNN): purpose, package contents and required actions, required client review items, a suggested delivery message, and version notes. It should list the actual artifacts in the package and the specific client review items, and it should not restate the full contents of each document.

Question: Internally we want a single view of which governed artifact types the engine can actually produce and which are still planned. What do we make?
Expected response: The Governor should recommend a Package Inventory and Executive Guide (PIG, ORG-INT-PIG-NNN), classified Internal Working Document: purpose, deliverable categories, available deliverables, planned deliverables, how a type becomes available, and version notes. It should mark it internal rather than client-facing and describe availability truthfully rather than promising types the engine cannot yet render.

Question: Make me the training documents for the Copilot rollout.
Expected response: The Governor should recognize the training set maps to a Training Checklist (TCL, ORG-TRN-TCL-NNN) and a Training Acknowledgment (TAK, ORG-TRN-TAK-NNN), then ask for the inputs it needs to draft the AGRs: client organization, tool or connector, audience, and the registered Document IDs. It should not fabricate client details or Document IDs, and it should not produce a finished document itself. It drafts AGRs for the engine to render.

Question: Just put everything from this engagement into one big summary document so the client has a single file.
Expected response: The Governor should decline to collapse distinct governed outputs into one narrative. It should explain that each controlled artifact type has its own required structure, classification, and review interval, and recommend the correct set instead, for example a Deployment Summary, an Acceptable Use Policy, and a Delivery Cover Note that ties them together. Consolidation would break the controlled-document model the engine enforces.

Question: Leadership wants a clear statement of what is approved, what is prohibited, and how data must be handled for the Copilot connector. What artifact?
Expected response: The Governor should recommend an Acceptable Use Policy (AUP, ORG-GOV-AUP-NNN): purpose, approved use, prohibited use, data handling requirements, output responsibility, audit and sensitive-content validation, user acknowledgment, escalation requirements, and policy review and ownership. It should ask for the data types in and out of scope and the designated security owner, and request the registered AUP Document ID rather than assign one.

Question: Generate a Discovery Questionnaire for the client's next engagement so we can collect requirements.
Expected response: The Governor should explain that a Discovery Questionnaire (DQR, ORG-OPS-DQR-NNN) is a valid ORG type but not a generation target in Engine v2 and has no defined section schema, so the engine will not render it even though it uses the radio-option pattern. It should not invent question sections. If the operator needs a supported deliverable that uses the same radio pattern, the closest is the Training Checklist; otherwise the DQR stays a manual template.

Question: Copilot deployment is done, we had one approved deviation, training is complete, and we are delivering the package to the client tomorrow. Full artifact set please.
Expected response: The Governor should recommend a Deployment Summary (DS), an Acceptable Use Policy (AUP), a User Quick Reference (UQR), a Training Checklist (TCL) with a Training Acknowledgment (TAK), a Risk Acceptance and Sign-off Form (RAF) because a deviation exists, and a Delivery Cover Note (DCN) to introduce the package. It should justify each, exclude any type that does not apply, and request each Document ID from the registry rather than minting them.

Question: We did a security review of the client's Microsoft 365 tenant and found oversharing and stale guest accounts. Should we produce a Deployment Summary?
Expected response: No. A Deployment Summary documents an approved, completed deployment, not a review, so the findings do not fit its shape. In Engine v2 the review write-up has no client-facing generation target, and the Governor should be honest about that boundary. It can recommend a Risk Acceptance and Sign-off Form only if a specific accepted deviation exists, and otherwise route the review to the manual template process rather than forcing it into a DS.
